introduction.name: Introduction to Data Structures
introduction.definition: A Data Structure is a specialized format for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data in computer memory so that operations can be performed efficiently.
introduction.classification: Data structures are broadly categorized into Primitive (integers, floats, characters, pointers) and Non-Primitive (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues, Trees, Graphs). Non-primitive structures are further divided into Linear and Non-Linear.
characteristics: Correctness: Retains data integrity across all operations.
Time Efficiency: Minimizes CPU execution time for insertions, deletions, and lookups.
Space Efficiency: Minimizes memory overhead and avoids memory fragmentation.

viva_questions.q: What is the difference between an Abstract Data Type (ADT) and a Data Structure?
viva_questions.a: An ADT specifies WHAT operations can be performed and what mathematical behaviors are expected (e.g., Stack ADT requires push and pop), while a Data Structure is the concrete implementation in code showing HOW operations are realized in memory.

viva_questions.q: What are linear vs non-linear data structures?
viva_questions.a: Linear data structures (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues) arrange elements sequentially where each element has a single predecessor and successor. Non-linear structures (Trees, Graphs) arrange elements hierarchically or interconnectedly where an element can have multiple predecessors or successors.

linear_vs_non_linear.name: Linear vs Non-Linear Data Structures
linear_vs_non_linear.definition: Linear data structures store elements sequentially in a single level, while Non-Linear data structures store elements in multi-level, hierarchical, or interconnected relationships.
linear_vs_non_linear.comparison_table:
| Parameter | Linear Data Structures | Non-Linear Data Structures |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Arrangement** | Sequential / Single-level | Multi-level / Hierarchical / Network |
| **Traversal** | Single pass can visit all elements | Multiple traversal orders (DFS, BFS, Inorder) |
| **Memory Allocation** | Mostly contiguous (Arrays) or linear pointers | Tree nodes / Graph adjacency lists |
| **Examples** | Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues | Binary Trees, BST, Heaps, Graphs |
| **Time Complexity** | Search is O(n) (O(log n) if sorted array) | BST Search is O(log n), Graph traversal O(V+E) |
| **Applications** | Buffer queues, undo stacks, sequential lists | File systems, hierarchy trees, network routing |
linear_vs_non_linear.explanation: Linear structures are easier to implement and navigate sequentially from start to end. Non-linear structures excel when modeling real-world hierarchical relationships (like folder trees, corporate org charts) or network relationships (like social graphs, city road networks).

viva_questions.q: Give two examples of non-linear data structures.
Can all elements of a tree be traversed in a single linear pass?
viva_questions.a: No, non-linear structures require traversal algorithms like Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, or Breadth-First Search (Level-Order) using auxiliary stacks or queues.

static_vs_dynamic_memory.name: Static vs Dynamic Memory Allocation
static_vs_dynamic_memory.definition: Static memory allocation allocates a fixed block of memory at compile time in the stack/data segment. Dynamic memory allocation allocates memory at runtime in the heap segment using standard functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free).
static_vs_dynamic_memory.comparison_table:
| Parameter | Static Memory Allocation | Dynamic Memory Allocation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Time of Allocation** | Compile time | Run time |
| **Memory Region** | Stack or Data Segment | Heap Segment |
| **Size Flexibility** | Fixed, cannot be resized | Resizable using realloc() |
| **Deallocation** | Automatic when out of scope | Manual via free() (Risk of memory leak) |
| **Efficiency** | Faster execution | Slight allocation overhead |
| **Example** | `int arr[100];` | `int *ptr = (int *)malloc(n * sizeof(int));` |

viva_questions.q: What is a memory leak and how do you prevent it in C?
viva_questions.a: A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated heap memory (via malloc/calloc) is no longer needed but is not released using free(). It is prevented by always pairing every malloc() with free() and setting the pointer to NULL.

viva_questions.q: What is the difference between malloc() and calloc()?
viva_questions.a: malloc(size) allocates a single uninitialized block containing garbage values. calloc(num, size) allocates memory for an array of elements and initializes every byte to zero.
A dangling pointer is a pointer that points to a memory location that has already been deallocated using free(). Accessing it causes undefined behavior or Segmentation Fault.

arrays_and_pointers.name: Arrays, Pointers, and Structures in C
arrays_and_pointers.definition: An array is a collection of homogeneous elements stored at contiguous memory locations. A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. A structure is a user-defined composite data type grouping heterogeneous elements.
arrays_and_pointers.explanation: In C, an array name decays into a pointer to its first element: `arr == &arr[0]`. Pointer arithmetic allows moving through array indices: `*(arr + i) == arr[i]`. In structures, members are accessed via dot `.` on direct variables or arrow `->` on struct pointers.

viva_questions.q: How is a 2D array stored in memory in C?
viva_questions.a: In C, 2D arrays are stored in Row-Major order where all elements of row 0 are placed first, followed by row 1, etc. Formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + (i * TotalColumns + j) * ElementSize.

viva_questions.q: What does the -> operator do in C?
viva_questions.a: The arrow operator `ptr->member` is syntactic shorthand for dereferencing a structure pointer and accessing its member: `(*ptr).member`.

asymptotic_notations.name: Asymptotic Notations (Big O, Omega, Theta)
asymptotic_notations.definition: Asymptotic notations are mathematical tools used to describe the limiting behavior and efficiency of an algorithm's running time or space requirements as the input size n grows towards infinity.
asymptotic_notations.comparison_table:
| Notation | Formal Definition | Mathematical Meaning | Practical Usage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Big O (O)** | f(n) <= c * g(n) for all n >= n0 | Asymptotic **Upper Bound** | Represents worst-case running time guarantee |
| **Big Omega (Ω)** | f(n) >= c * g(n) for all n >= n0 | Asymptotic **Lower Bound** | Represents best-case minimum execution time |
| **Big Theta (Θ)** | c1*g(n) <= f(n) <= c2*g(n) | Asymptotic **Tight Bound** | Exact growth rate when upper & lower match |
asymptotic_notations.growth_hierarchy: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(n^3) < O(2^n) < O(n!)
asymptotic_notations.explanation: Big O gives the worst-case upper bound guarantee — the algorithm will NEVER perform worse than this. Big Omega gives the best-case lower bound — the algorithm will require AT LEAST this many steps. Big Theta gives the tight bound when upper and lower bounds coincide.

viva_questions.q: Why is Big O preferred over Big Omega in software engineering?
viva_questions.a: Big O provides a safe upper bound guarantee (worst-case scenario), ensuring system limits, SLA deadlines, and memory budgets are never breached.

viva_questions.q: What is the difference between Big O and Big Theta?
viva_questions.a: Big O is an upper bound (it can be loose, e.g. an O(n) algorithm is technically also O(n^2)), while Big Theta represents an asymptotically tight bound where upper and lower bounds match.
